plainLanguage: For the same relative load, a standing cable cross-over put a larger turning force on the shoulder joint than a flat barbell bench press.
qualifiers: The cable cross-over in this study is not the index cable fly: pulley height was not reported, the elbow angle was not prescribed and stance was not described, so it is a related condition.
Loads were set as a percentage of body weight rather than of 1RM, so the relative intensity of the two exercises is unknown and may differ.
The shoulder was modelled as the humerus relative to the thorax with no separate scapula, which the authors name as their key limitation.
A joint moment is an external mechanical demand, not a muscle force and not a growth stimulus.

conditions: loads of 15 and 30 per cent of body weight, six repetitions per condition, laboratory motion capture with cable load cells
scope.population: twenty healthy adults aged 18 to 45 with at least two hours per week of weight-training experience, ten male and ten female

Abstract (static optimisation underestimates antagonist activity at the glenohumeral joint)

statement: At matched external loads of 15 and 30 per cent of body weight, a standing cable cross-over produced significantly larger maximum absolute shoulder joint moments than a flat barbell bench press: 0.650 (SD 0.113) against 0.442 (SD 0.046) Nm/kg at 15 per cent of body weight, and 1.026 (SD 0.192) against 0.760 (SD 0.079) Nm/kg at 30 per cent.
